Which of the following gives the length of the curve $y=\frac{{x}^{2}}{4}$ for $x\in [-3,4],$ as shown above?
questions.worked_solution:
The arc length of a curve $y=f(x)$ between $x=a$ and $x=b$ can be found using the formula

$$
L={\int }_{a}^{b}\sqrt{1+[{f}^{′}(x)]^{2}}\,\text{d}x.
$$

In our case, $f(x)=\frac{{x}^{2}}{4},$ $a=-3,$ and $b=4.$

First, we find the derivative of $f(x):$

$$
{f}^{′}(x)=\frac{2x}{4}=\frac{x}{2}
$$

Substituting ${f}^{′}(x)=\frac{x}{2}$ into the arc length formula, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}L & ={\int }_{-3}^{4}\sqrt{1+{[{f}^{′}(x)]}^{2}}\,\text{d}x \\  & ={\int }_{-3}^{4}\sqrt{1+\frac{{x}^{2}}{4}}\,\text{d}x \\  & =\frac{1}{2}{\int }_{-3}^{4}\sqrt{{x}^{2}+4}\,\text{d}x.\end{aligned}
$$

questions.problem: The length of the curve $y={cos}^{2}⁡x$ on $[0,\pi ]$ is given by
questions.worked_solution:
The arc length of a curve $y=f(x)$ between $x=a$ and $x=b$ can be found using the formula

$$
L={\int }_{a}^{b}\sqrt{1+[{f}^{′}(x)]^{2}}\,\text{d}x.
$$

In our case, $f(x)={cos}^{2}⁡x,$ $a=0,$ and $b=\pi .$

First, we find the derivative of $f(x):$

$$
{f}^{′}(x)=-2\operatorname{cos}⁡x\operatorname{sin}⁡x=-\operatorname{sin}⁡(2x)
$$

Substituting ${f}^{′}(x)=-\operatorname{sin}⁡2x$ into the arc length formula, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}L & ={\int }_{0}^{\pi }\sqrt{1+[{f}^{′}(x)]^{2}}\,\text{d}x \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{\pi }\sqrt{1+(-\operatorname{sin}⁡(2x))^{2}}\,\text{d}x \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{\pi }\sqrt{1+{sin}^{2}⁡(2x)}\,\text{d}x.\end{aligned}
$$

questions.problem: Compute the arc length of $y=\frac{2\sqrt{2}}{3}{x}^{3/2}$ for $x\in [0,4].$
questions.worked_solution:
The arc length of a curve $y=f(x)$ between two points where $x=a$ and $x=b$ can be found using the formula:

$$
L={\int }_{a}^{b}\sqrt{1+[{f}^{′}(x)]^{2}}\,\text{d}x.
$$

In our case, $f(x)=\frac{2\sqrt{2}}{3}{x}^{3/2},$ $a=0,$ and $b=4.$

First, we find the derivative of $f(x):$

$$
{f}^{′}(x)=\sqrt{2x}
$$

Substituting ${f}^{′}(x)=\sqrt{2x}$ to the formula for the arc length, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}L & ={\int }_{0}^{4}\sqrt{1+[{f}^{′}(x)]^{2}}\,\text{d}x \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{4}\sqrt{1+[\sqrt{2x}]^{2}}\,\text{d}x \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{4}\sqrt{1+2x}\,\text{d}x.\end{aligned}
$$

We evaluate this integral using the substitution $u=1+2x.$ Then, $\text{d}x=\frac{1}{2}\text{d}u.$

We also need to compute new limits:

$$
\begin{aligned}x & 0 & 4 \\ u & 1 & 9\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}L & ={\int }_{1}^{9}\sqrt{u}\cdot \frac{1}{2}\,\text{d}u \\  & =\frac{1}{2}{\int }_{1}^{9}\sqrt{u}\,\text{d}x \\  & =\frac{1}{2}{[\frac{2}{3}{u}^{3/2}]|}_{1}^{9} \\  & =\frac{1}{3}({9}^{3/2}-{1}^{3/2}) \\  & =\frac{27-1}{3} \\  & =\frac{26}{3}.\end{aligned}
$$

questions.problem: Compute the arc length of $y=\frac{2}{3}(x-1)^{3/2}$ for $x\in [1,4].$
questions.worked_solution:
The arc length of a curve $y=f(x)$ between $x=a$ and $x=b$ can be found using the formula

$$
L={\int }_{a}^{b}\sqrt{1+[{f}^{′}(x)]^{2}}\,\text{d}x.
$$

In our case, $f(x)=\frac{2}{3}(x-1)^{3/2},$ $a=1,$ and $b=4.$

First, we find the derivative of $f(x):$

$$
{f}^{′}(x)=\frac{2}{3}\cdot \frac{3}{2}(x-1)^{1/2}=\sqrt{x-1}
$$

Now, let's compute $\sqrt{1+[{f}^{′}(x)]^{2}}:$

$$
\begin{aligned}\sqrt{1+[{f}^{′}(x)]^{2}} & =\sqrt{1+{(\sqrt{x-1})}^{2}} \\  & =\sqrt{1+x-1} \\  & =\sqrt{x}\end{aligned}
$$

Substituting $\sqrt{1+[{f}^{′}(x)]^{2}}=\sqrt{x}$ to the formula for the arc length, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}L & ={\int }_{1}^{4}\sqrt{x}\,\text{d}x \\  & ={[\frac{2}{3}{x}^{3/2}]|}_{1}^{4} \\  & =\frac{2}{3}({4}^{3/2}-{1}^{3/2}) \\  & =\frac{2(8-1)}{3} \\  & =\frac{14}{3}.\end{aligned}
$$
